strengths: Addresses an important NLP safety problem: scalable construction of domain-specific harmful prompts that are less explicit than standard benchmark queries.
The end-to-end pipeline is clearly presented, spans four high-stakes domains, and includes comparisons across several open and proprietary target models.
The paper reports useful analyses beyond attack success, including fluency, diversity, safety fine-tuning, model-scale comparisons, and limited ablations of rewriting paths and iteration budgets.
Appendices provide root entities, thresholds, hyperparameters, example prompts, and generation templates, improving transparency.
weaknesses: The central claims of realistic implicitness and domain relevance are not adequately validated. There is no human evaluation of realism, implicitness, intent preservation, domain expertise, or prompt quality; examples often resemble conspicuous jargon substitution rather than natural covert requests.

Evidence for the knowledge-graph contribution is especially weak. Its sole ablation reports Self-BLEU, without measuring domain coverage, relevance, harmfulness, ASR, or comparison to simpler entity lists/retrieval. The Self-BLEU values in Appendix Table 11 also do not align clearly with the main cross-domain results.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on LLM classifiers and judges. Judge prompts, exact model versions, agreement statistics, human validation, confidence intervals, and repeated-run variability are missing. Harmfulness above 95% is largely tautological because the same type of score is used to filter examples at a 0.9 threshold.

RA-Implicit-success is selected for successful attacks on one target and then compared with unselected public datasets, making that comparison intrinsically favorable. More broadly, the most relevant domain-specific baseline, TRIDENT, is excluded, while comparisons primarily use general-domain benchmarks.

The safety-fine-tuning experiment lacks documented train/test splits and controls for paired or near-duplicate explicit and rewritten prompts. Consequently, its improvements may reflect leakage between variants rather than generalization to unseen covert harms. The harmful-refusal response construction is also insufficiently specified.

Reproducibility remains inadequate: the training data and procedure used to create the fine-tuned synthesis and rewriting models are not described, several proprietary models are underspecified, judge templates are absent, graph sizes are unreported, and only one of the claimed graph-relation queries is shown.

The dual-path advantage is modest and unsupported by uncertainty estimates: at 10 and 18 iterations it only narrowly exceeds direct rewriting. The manuscript's stronger interpretation about escaping local optima is therefore speculative.

Claims of broad coverage, cross-domain generalization, and real-world threat fidelity exceed the evidence. Four independently constructed domains do not demonstrate generalization to unseen domains, and no real-user or expert-curated distribution is used for comparison. These issues require substantial new validation before the work is sound and reproducible enough for Findings.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important NLP safety problem: scalable construction of domain-specific harmful prompts, including covert formulations that may evade lexical safety mechanisms. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/a928ef3f8cce43df9b497903c4f5becf/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The proposed pipeline is coherent and reasonably well documented, with equations, pseudocode, generation templates, knowledge-graph queries, hyperparameters, representative examples, and evaluations spanning six target models and four domains.

The experiments provide some evidence that the generated prompts transfer beyond the Llama model used during rewriting: the unfiltered implicit set achieves substantially higher measured ASR than both its explicit counterpart and the selected public benchmarks.
The safety-fine-tuning experiment is a useful attempt to demonstrate downstream value rather than reporting attack success alone, and the paper reports capability results alongside safety results.
weaknesses: The central claim that RiskAtlas produces realistic, implicit, semantically faithful prompts is not adequately validated. There is no human evaluation, annotation protocol, inter-annotator agreement, or validated automatic implicitness measure. Several examples remain overtly malicious and are phrased in conspicuously unnatural technical jargon. Higher perplexity for the implicit variants reinforces this concern rather than establishing realism.

Evaluation is almost entirely circular and model-mediated. LLMs generate the prompts, judge intent preservation and fluency, determine harmfulness, and score attack success, yet the paper provides no human audit or evidence that these judges agree with qualified annotators. The quality model Mqual is not identified, its prompts and decision reliability are not analyzed, and the reported greater-than-95% harmfulness is partly a consequence of filtering with the same Granite Guardian model used for evaluation.

RA-Implicit-checkmark is a selected subset defined by successful attacks and therefore is not a fair benchmark for headline comparison; its very high ASR is partly tautological. Even for the unfiltered set, comparisons against general-purpose explicit benchmarks confound domain, harm distribution, explicitness, prompt length, and generation procedure. Only 200 prompts per dataset are evaluated, with no confidence intervals, repeated sampling, or significance testing.

The evidence for the knowledge graph—the distinguishing component in the title—is particularly weak. Its only ablation reports Self-BLEU, which neither establishes domain relevance nor shows improved risk coverage, semantic validity, or attack effectiveness. There is no comparison against simpler entity lists, Wikipedia retrieval, taxonomies, or non-graph prompting, so the results do not demonstrate that graph structure is necessary.

The dual-path contribution is also weakly supported. At the default iteration budget of 10, dual-path OSR is only 29.03% versus 28.25% for direct rewriting, without uncertainty estimates; the context-card path is worse. Larger gains appear only at budgets not used in the main experiments. Consequently, the ablation does not convincingly support the claimed advantage of the principal methodological design.

The safety fine-tuning evaluation does not specify independent train/test splits. RiskAtlas variants are transformations of the same source prompts, so training on RA-Origin and testing on RA-Implicit, or vice versa, may leak entities and underlying intents. Refusal targets are also unspecified. Moreover, every alignment condition loses roughly 6–7 MMLU points, making the claim of capability preservation misleading: the result establishes only comparable degradation across datasets.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite extensive appendices. The paper does not clearly report graph sizes, generated and retained sample counts, model-training data for the synthesis and obfuscation models, the exact quality model, dataset splits, refusal-response construction, judge prompts, or API snapshots. A fixed seed does not control proprietary APIs, and no variance across generation or judging runs is reported.

Claims that the dataset reflects real-world threats and that the method generalizes across domains exceed the evidence. The four domains are all directly included during construction, no unseen-domain transfer is tested, and no empirical sample of real user attacks is used to establish realism. A directly relevant domain-specific benchmark, TRIDENT, is excluded rather than adapted for a controlled comparison.

Overall, the idea is relevant and potentially recoverable, but establishing the paper's main claims requires substantial new validation: blinded human assessment, independent test construction, stronger KG and dual-path baselines, uncertainty analysis, and complete reproducibility details. The current evidence is insufficient for Findings-level soundness.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important ACL-relevant problem: constructing domain-specific safety data whose harmful intent is less lexically explicit. The combination of knowledge-graph grounding and iterative rewriting is coherent and potentially useful.

The evaluation has meaningful breadth: four domains, six independently held-out target models, open- and closed-source systems, three ASR judges, cross-model rewriting results, and a downstream safety-tuning experiment.

The large transfer-ASR increase for RA-Implicit over RA-Origin is consistent across every evaluated target model. This supports the narrower claim that the rewriting pipeline produces prompts that evade current safety mechanisms more often than explicit prompts.
The paper includes helpful ablations of rewriting paths and iteration budgets, representative examples, generation templates, graph-query details, and many training and inference hyperparameters.

The manuscript is clearly structured and generally easy to follow. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/1e19f3b6125e484e8d031c4da2d86613/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central dataset-quality claims—domain relevance, preservation of harmful intent, implicitness, realism, and fluency—receive no human validation. They are inferred from LLM judgments, Granite-Guardian scores, embedding similarity, perplexity, and ASR, none of which directly establishes all these properties. Several presented “implicit” examples remain conspicuously harmful or use unnatural technical euphemisms, weakening the realism claim.

The benchmark comparison is not well controlled. RiskAtlas is an adversarially rewritten resource, whereas the principal baselines are mostly explicit harmful-prompt datasets. The paper omits direct comparisons with the closely related obfuscation methods discussed in its own related-work section and excludes TRIDENT on the grounds that it uses jailbreak-based generation, even though RiskAtlas itself iteratively uses target-model outcomes and failure feedback.

RA-Implicit-success is explicitly selected for successful obfuscation against Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, so its very high transfer ASR is informative about transfer but not a fair estimate for an unselected benchmark distribution. The paper sometimes treats this success-conditioned subset as an ordinary dataset variant without sufficiently emphasizing the selection effect.

Evidence for the knowledge graph's contribution is particularly weak. The sole guided-versus-unguided ablation reports Self-BLEU, which measures lexical overlap rather than domain relevance, semantic coverage, risk discovery, or prompt quality. Root selection and sitelink thresholds are heuristic and unvalidated, and basic graph/dataset statistics such as node counts, candidate counts, filtering attrition, and final dataset sizes are absent.

The claimed advantage of dual-path rewriting is small at the default budget (29.03% versus 28.25% OSR for direct rewriting) and virtually absent at 18 iterations. No repeated runs, confidence intervals, significance tests, or human inspection establish that these differences are reliable.

The safety-tuning evidence is difficult to interpret without explicit train/test separation and deduplication across RA-Origin and its derived implicit variants; overlap could substantially inflate robustness. All results appear to use one seed and only 200 training examples. Moreover, every safety-tuned model loses roughly 6–7 MMLU points, so describing capability as “preserved” is too strong, even if the degradation is similar across datasets.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the release claim: the manuscript contains a GitHub footnote marker but no visible URL or PDF hyperlink, several operational details and judge prompts are missing, and crucial evaluation depends on changing proprietary models. The method narrative is also internally inconsistent: it claims target responses are used only for early stopping rather than optimization, while Algorithm 1 and Appendix I feed failure information and trigger words into subsequent rewrites.

Overall, the promising ASR findings justify borderline Findings consideration, but the unsupported dataset-quality claims, baseline mismatch, possible evaluation leakage, and incomplete reproducibility prevent a clear soundness recommendation in the current version. Human validation, fair obfuscation baselines, documented disjoint splits, uncertainty estimates, and an accessible release could plausibly resolve these concerns next cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP-safety problem: scalable construction of domain-grounded harmful prompts, including indirect formulations that surface-level safety filters may miss.

The proposed pipeline is coherent and clearly presented, combining Wikidata-based entity retrieval, category-conditioned synthesis, filtering, and iterative obfuscation. Prompt templates, graph roots, thresholds, and many training parameters are included.

Evaluation covers four domains and several open and proprietary target models. The large transfer gains of SG-Implicit over SG-Origin suggest that indirect wording exposes genuine weaknesses beyond the model used during rewriting.

The paper includes useful supplementary checks: comparisons with additional jailbreak datasets, two defenses, StrongREJECT evaluation, cross-backbone generation results, a downstream safety-tuning experiment, and limited component ablations.
Testing the generated data as both a red-teaming resource and safety-training resource is valuable and relevant to the claimed practical use case.
weaknesses: The central claims of high-quality, realistic, domain-specific data are not adequately validated. There is no human or domain-expert assessment of harmful-intent preservation, domain relevance, realism, implicitness, or annotation reliability. All decisive quality judgments are automated, and the representative examples are often conspicuously euphemistic rather than demonstrably realistic user requests.

Attack success is confounded with the generation procedure. Despite claiming that target responses are used only for early stopping, the appendix prompt explicitly feeds back refusal types, trigger words, banned words, and a target response across iterations. This is target-conditioned jailbreak optimization, not merely an efficiency criterion, and the methodological description understates that dependence.

SG-Implicit-checkmark is a success-selected subset, so comparing it directly with unselected public benchmarks predictably inflates ASR. Even SG-Implicit is generated through feedback from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Cross-model transfer is informative, but it does not make the selected-subset comparison a fair measure of dataset quality.

The KG contribution is weakly isolated. Its only reported ablation measures Self-BLEU, with values inconsistent with the main cross-domain table, and does not test domain relevance, risk coverage, harmfulness, ASR, or performance against simpler entity lists or unstructured retrieval. Consequently, the evidence does not establish that graph structure materially drives the reported gains.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates, repeated sampling, significance tests, and sensitivity to sampled benchmark subsets. With only 200 prompts per condition, these omissions limit confidence in many comparisons.

Reproducibility is insufficient for Findings as submitted. The paper does not report the complete dataset size, per-stage retention counts, synthesis-model training data, identity/configuration of the quality model, exact judge prompts, or key failure-feedback extraction details. It claims a GitHub release but provides no accessible link, while several core evaluations depend on version-sensitive proprietary APIs.

The safety-fine-tuning study does not measure benign-query refusal or helpfulness, so reduced ASR could reflect broad over-refusal. MMLU is not an adequate substitute, and all fine-tuned models lose roughly 6–7 absolute MMLU points, which conflicts with the paper's favorable capability-preservation framing.

The paper repeatedly equates higher ASR with better stealth and realism, but ASR can also arise from judge errors, category mismatch, or unusually technical wording. The all-LLM judging setup, without human calibration or reported agreement, leaves this alternative explanation unresolved.

Claims of systematic domain coverage and identification of high-risk concepts are unsupported by graph statistics, coverage analyses, or comparisons with expert taxonomies. Popularity-based Wikidata filtering may favor well-known entities while excluding precisely the specialized risks the paper aims to expose.

Overall, the work shows a promising data-generation approach, but substantial evaluation and reporting revisions are needed to establish its central claims and make the contribution reproducible; it is therefore better suited to resubmission than a borderline Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP safety problem: scalable construction of domain-specific, implicitly harmful prompts rather than only overt attacks.
The proposed pipeline is understandable and combines knowledge-graph grounding, harmfulness and fluency filtering, and iterative rewriting in a coherent end-to-end framework.

Evaluation covers four domains, several open and proprietary target models, safety fine-tuning, two defense mechanisms, an alternative StrongREJECT evaluation, and comparisons with both standard harmful-prompt datasets and jailbreak benchmarks.
The appendices provide generation templates, an example SPARQL query, model settings, thresholds, and several ablations, which is more documentation than is typical for a purely synthetic-data paper.
weaknesses: The central claim that the resulting prompts are realistic, domain-relevant, semantically faithful, and high quality is not adequately validated. There is no human evaluation, domain-expert assessment, annotation protocol, or inter-annotator agreement. Harmfulness classifiers, embedding similarity, perplexity, and LLM judges cannot establish these properties. Several displayed rewrites are awkward jargon substitutions rather than plausible real-world requests.

The strongest reported variant, SG-Implicit✓, is explicitly selected for successfully attacking a target model. Its much higher ASR is therefore partly a consequence of outcome-based selection, making comparisons with unselected public datasets misleading. Transfer to other models is useful evidence, but it does not remove this selection advantage or establish superior dataset quality.

The knowledge graph's contribution is weakly supported. The only reported KG ablation uses Self-BLEU, without evaluating domain relevance, risk coverage, harmfulness, or downstream ASR. The Self-BLEU values in this ablation also do not align transparently with those in the main cross-domain table. No graph sizes, retained-node counts, coverage analysis, or comparison against simpler entity lists or text retrieval is provided.

Claims of cross-domain generalization are overstated: the method is instantiated and evaluated on four development domains, with no held-out-domain transfer experiment. Popularity-based Wikidata filtering may exclude rare but important risks, and examples such as treating pedophilia as a medical node illustrate that graph proximity does not itself establish a meaningful domain-specific risk.

The safety fine-tuning study uses only 200 examples, apparently one seed, and reports no uncertainty or significance tests. Dataset construction for the refusal pairs is insufficiently described. Table 3 omits each StealthGraph variant's diagonal evaluation and then reports column averages over unequal test sets, weakening the claimed comparative advantage. The roughly seven-point MMLU decline is also substantial despite being described as capability preservation.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the release claim. The manuscript provides no identifiable repository or artifact, full datasets, complete queries for all domains and relations, exact model/version identifiers, synthesis fine-tuning data, identity and prompt of the quality model, refusal-generation procedure, or all generation counts and retention statistics. Proprietary judges further make exact reproduction difficult.

The method description is internally underspecified: Algorithm 1 does not show the failure-feedback update described in the prose, the two rewriting paths and state updates are unclear, and the final-candidate rule is described as selecting the highest-quality candidate although the algorithm simply returns the most recent accepted candidate.

Baseline fairness is questionable. The main comparison emphasizes mostly explicit harmful-prompt datasets, whereas StealthGraph actively performs iterative target-informed obfuscation. Appendix comparisons help, but generation budgets, selection protocols, domains, and prompt distributions are not controlled, so higher ASR alone does not demonstrate a better benchmark.

The paper interprets small harm-category frequency differences as meaningful domain patterns without statistical testing, even though categories are directly imposed during generation. More broadly, no confidence intervals or repeated-sampling results are reported for the 200-item evaluations.

Overall, the idea and experimental breadth are promising, but substantial new validation and clearer experimental controls are needed before the work meets the soundness and reproducibility threshold for Findings. A next-cycle revision appears feasible if it adds expert human validation, fair matched baselines, complete artifacts, stronger KG ablations, uncertainty estimates, and corrected fine-tuning comparisons.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important, clearly motivated NLP safety problem: scalable construction of covert, domain-specific harmful prompts. The two-stage framework is coherent and presented clearly, with useful examples and formalization. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/2aa387b9b0dc45b88a986424a04f196e/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical study is broader than a minimal benchmark demonstration: it covers four domains, multiple open and proprietary target models, three-judge voting, StrongREJECT, two defenses, transfer to models not used during rewriting, and a downstream safety-tuning experiment.

The substantial transfer gains of SG-Implicit over SG-Origin provide credible evidence that indirect wording exposes weaknesses missed by explicit prompts. Evaluating on models distinct from the rewriting target strengthens this result.

The appendices disclose root nodes, thresholds, decoding and LoRA settings, a SPARQL query, generation and rewriting templates, examples, and additional comparisons. These materials improve transparency.
The paper usefully evaluates both adversarial effectiveness and downstream defensive utility rather than treating attack success alone as the contribution.
weaknesses: The central dataset-quality claims are not adequately validated. There is no human evaluation—especially no domain-expert assessment—of harmful-intent preservation, domain relevance, naturalness, realism, or whether prompts are genuinely implicit. PPL, cosine similarity, Self-BLEU, automated harmfulness scores, and attack success are not substitutes for these judgments. Several examples read as conspicuous technical synonym substitution rather than realistic user queries.

Evidence for the knowledge graph's contribution is particularly weak. The only KG ablation reports Self-BLEU, without measuring domain relevance, entity/risk coverage, harmfulness, ASR, or downstream alignment. There is no comparison against flat entity retrieval, Wikipedia descriptions, or randomly sampled concepts. Consequently, the paper does not establish that graph structure—rather than simply supplying entity names and descriptions—drives the gains.

The strongest headline results use SG-Implicit✓, a subset selected for successful attacks on the rewriting target, while comparison datasets are not subjected to analogous success-conditioned selection. This makes its ASR advantage partly circular. Even SG-Implicit comparisons are confounded by unmatched domains, harm categories, and generation procedures; no uncertainty intervals or significance tests are reported for samples of only 200 prompts.

The claimed advantage of the two-strategy rewriting design is limited. At the chosen ten-iteration setting, it achieves 29.03% OSR versus 28.25% for direct rewriting, while the context-card path is worse. The larger-budget gains are modest and lack repeated-run uncertainty. Thus, the evidence does not strongly support the context-card component as a substantive innovation.

The safety-fine-tuning study is difficult to interpret: train/test splits and entity or prompt-family overlap are not specified, the missing diagonal entries suggest direct overlap concerns, and only 200 refusal pairs are used. The roughly 6–7-point absolute MMLU decline relative to the untuned model also makes the claim of capability preservation too strong, even if the decline is similar across datasets.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the detailed appendix. The manuscript promises a GitHub release but provides no accessible URL or artifact; it does not fully identify the synthesis fine-tuning data, quality model, judge and semantic-preservation prompts, dataset construction counts and exclusions, safety-SFT configuration, exact proprietary-model versions, or Wikidata snapshot. Algorithm 1 also omits parts of the stated failure-feedback and candidate-ranking procedure.

Overall, the approach is promising and the transfer evidence is encouraging, but the missing independent validation and weak causal evidence for the KG and two-strategy components prevent a clear Findings recommendation. These concerns appear addressable in a revision through expert annotation, matched evaluations, stronger ablations, held-out safety-tuning splits, uncertainty reporting, and a complete artifact release.
